newsitem.title: FRANCE: Two decades on, France's Malraux stops smoking.
newsitem.headline: Two decades on, France's Malraux stops smoking.

text.p: Twenty years after his death, French writer, adventurer and culture minister Andre Malraux has given up smoking for a new postage stamp.

A thumb-nail portrait on a new commemorative stamp copies a famous 1935 photograph of a stern, inquisitive-looking Malraux, hair dishevelled by the wind -- except that the cigarette in the corner of his mouth has gone.
The Post Office said 1991 French laws cracking down on smoking meant Malraux, who was President Charles de Gaulle's culture minister, had to abstain in public to avoid seeming to encourage smoking.

"The Post Office cannot have a picture of a smoker alongside the words 'French Republic' on a stamp," said Madeleine Mazet, a Post Office spokeswoman on Thursday. "But Malraux without his cigarette is still Malraux."

The stamp is due out on the 20th anniversary of his death on November 23, when he is to be reburied as a national hero at the Paris Pantheon, the last resting place of such illustrious figures as Voltaire, Rousseau or Victor Hugo.

Malraux, who travelled widely, drew on his real-life adventures for his best known works "La Condition Humaine" (Man's Estate) about revolutionary tensions in China in the 1920s and L'Espoir (Hope) after setting up a squadron of foreign pilots for the Republicans in Spain's Civil War.
Mazet said the Post Office had similarly snatched a pipe from the late French-born composer Arthur Honegger for a 1992 stamp marking the centenary of his birth.

She said fictional characters fared better. Georges Simenon's detective Inspector Maigret had been allowed to smoke on stamps. And Fantomas, an endearing French turn-of-the-century crook, had even been allowed to carry a dagger.
